# Iron(III)-Mediated C–H Alkylation: One-Electron Differentiation Increases Activity and Chemoselectivity

**Authors:** Tianyi Zhang; William G. Whitehurst; Matthew V. Pecoraro; Junho Kim; Stefan G. Koenig; Paul J. Chirik

**Affiliations:** a Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States | b Synthetic Molecule Process Chemistry, Genentech Inc, South San Francisco, California 94080, United States

## Abstract

The C–H functionalization of arenes mediated by well-defined bis(phosphine)-supported organometallic iron(III) complexes is described. One-electron oxidation of trans-(depe)2Fe(CH3)2 (depe = 1,2-bis(diethylphosphino)ethane) generated the corresponding isolable iron(III) dimethyl derivative that proved unstable towards Fe–CH3 homolysis. Oxidation of the corresponding iron(II) bis(aryl) complex, trans-(depe)2Fe(tolyl)2 resulted in rapid reductive elimination of the biaryl with formation of iron(I). These observations motivated the synthesis of the cationic iron(III) metallacycle derived from C–H activation of a neophyl ligand. This complex mediated the ortho-selective C(sp2)–H alkylation of a host of arene derivatives containing ketone, amide, pyridine, ester and sulfoxide directing groups with greater selectivity and reactivity than the iron(II) counterpart. The effect of bis(phosphine) ligands was examined, where decreasing ligand lability correlated with a higher barrier. The experimental rate law, deuterium labeling studies, deuterium kinetic isotope effect experiments and computational modeling support a reversible C–H activation step followed by rate-determining C(sp2)–C(sp3) reductive elimination. Using design principles to minimize undesired reactivity, the iron(III) cycloneophyl complex mediated more facile and chemoselective C–H functionalization with a broader directing group compatibility than the iron(II) analog, arising from a combination of increased ligand lability, less exergonic substrate coordination, enhanced orbital hybridization effect in C–H activation and more facile C–C reductive elimination.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

The transition-metal mediated, selective conversion of C–H to C–C(sp3) bonds is desirable with the potential to streamline organic synthesis and prepare C(sp3)-rich molecules.1 Precious metals have been extensively studied for C–H functionalization with well-established design principles for reactivity and selectivity, principally owing to their reliable and highly predictable redox chemistry.2 By comparison, related C–H functionalization reactions with more earth-abundant 3d transition metals, while documented, remain underdeveloped.3 Such reactions, particularly with iron, are attractive owing to the low cost,4 high natural abundance,5 and minimal toxicity of the metal.6

Despite early reports of the oxidative addition of aromatic C(sp2)–H bond by in-situ generated iron(0) intermediates,7 the full potential of iron-mediated C–H functionalization reactions has not been realized. Specifically, the higher density of states of the first-row metal and kinetically and thermodynamically more accessible one-electron differentiated oxidation states offer the potential for distinct reactivity over precious metals.8 As illustrated in Scheme 1, examples of C–H activation and functionalization with iron(0) and iron(II) complexes are the most well documented. For the former, cleavage of C–H bonds by in-situ generated four-coordinate bis(phosphine) iron(0) complexes was first reported by Miyake, Ittel and Tolman and coworkers.7 Empirical studies including transient and matrix photochemistry and isolation of oxidative addition intermediates have corroborated the concerted oxidative addition of C–H bonds at an iron(0) center as the commonly accepted pathway (Scheme 1A).9

By comparison, iron(II)-mediated C–H activation has been reported with complexes containing phosphines,10 cyclopentadienyls,11 and several strong-field supporting ligands.12 Based on computational studies and characterization of post C–H activation organometallic intermediates,13 a redox-neutral σ-complex-assisted metathesis (σ-CAM) mechanism featuring a concerted four-membered transition state has been proposed (Scheme 1B).14 A recent study by our laboratory has established the effects of ligand denticity and sterics, metal spin state, directing group and orbital hybridization on the reactivity and selectivity of iron(II)-mediated C–H functionalization through a combined experimental and computational study on a family of bis(phosphine) iron(II) complexes.15 Overall, iron(II)-mediated C–H functionalization proceeds through a redox-neutral σ-CAM pathway on the singlet surface, with C–H cleavage as the rate- and selectivity-determining step.15

C–H functionalization involving iron(III) complexes is by comparison rare (Scheme 1C) and typically proceeds by outer-sphere radical-mediated H-atom abstraction which does not occur directly at the iron(III) center.16 This includes Fenton chemistry where C–H bond breaking is mediated by free oxygen- or halogen-centered radicals generated from iron(III) precursors17,18 or by iron(III) imido and oxo/hydroxy/peroxy complexes.19,20 Other examples include deprotonation of benzylic C–H bonds by [(η5-C5R5)Fe(η6-arene)]2+ complexes,21 and C–H cleavage by gaseous iron(III) oxide ions and Fe-ZSM-5 zeolites.22

Organometallic iron(III) complexes have been invoked for inner-sphere C–H activation following treatment of iron(III) salts with Grignard, organozinc or organoaluminate activators.23 Illies, Shang, Nakamura and co-workers have proposed redox-neutral C–H activation by a putative iron(III) alkyl or aryl complex, assisted by chelation with picolinoylamide, N-(quinolin-8-yl)amide or other directing groups (Scheme 1D).23 Matsunaga and coworkers proposed an iron(III) metallacycle as the reactive intermediate responsible for directed C(sp2)–H activation of benzamides in the presence of a photocatalyst.24 Square-planar iron(III) alkyl and aryl complexes supported by a pyridine-2,6-dicarboxylamide pincer were proposed by Ghosh and coworkers as the active intermediate for C–H activation of tetrahydrofuran and furan derivatives.25 DFT computations by Chen and co-workers have also suggested a more facile directed C–H activation by bipyridine, bis(phosphine) or bis(NHC)-supported iron(III) complexes.26

Although organometallic iron(III) complexes have been proposed for C–H functionalization, experimental data is lacking and direct observation of such reactivity from well-defined precursors remains rare (Scheme 1C). 24,26,27 Building on precedents with iron(0) and iron(II), the synthesis, characterization and C(sp2)–H bond functionalization reactivity of observed and isolable bis(phosphine) iron(III) organometallic compounds is described (Chart 1). One-electron differentiated C–H functionalization reactivity between iron(III) and iron(II) was demonstrated and the key factors governing the reactivity and selectivity were outlined based on electronic structure determination and mechanistic studies by a combined experimental and computational approach. Overall, with careful design of the organometallic complex to minimize undesired reactivity, iron(III) complexes were found to promote more facile and selective C–H functionalization across a broader scope of directing groups.

## RESULTS

### Synthesis and Characterization of Cationic Iron(III) Dimethyl Complexes.

Due to the synthetic accessibility and the known C–H activation reactivity of their iron(II) counterparts,15,28 preparation of bis(phosphine)-supported iron(III) dimethyl complexes was initially targeted. Addition of one equivalent of [(η5-C5H5)2Fe][BArF4] to a diethyl ether solution containing one equivalent of (depe)2Fe(CH3)2 (1a) at ambient temperature resulted in an immediate color change from yellow to green (Scheme 2). Following concentration in vacuo and trituration in pentane, recrystallization in diethyl ether at −35 °C afforded olive-green crystals of [(depe)2Fe(CH3)2][BArF4] (2a) in 65% yield. The dmpe variant (dmpe = 1,2-bis(dimethylphosphino)ethane), 2b, was prepared in 61% yield from (dmpe)2Fe(CH3)2 (1b) using a similar procedure (see Supporting Information). The benzene-d6 1H NMR spectrum of 2a exhibits shifted and broadened resonances between 15 and 11 ppm as well as between 0 and −20 ppm, diagnostic of a paramagnetic iron(III) complex. The number of 1H NMR resonances for 2a and 2b are consistent with the presence of both cis and trans isomers, which is expected as the corresponding iron(II) complexes (1a and 1b) are also cis/trans mixtures.

The solid-state structure of the trans-2a was determined by X-ray diffraction and an idealized octahedral geometry was observed, confirming the identity of the compound (Figure 1A). Attempts to obtain the solid-state structure of cis-2a have been unsuccessful. Notably, the Fe–C bond distance in trans-2a, 2.097(4) Å, is shorter than the 2.183(3) Å in the iron(II) counterpart (trans-1a),15,28 likely a result of increased electrostatic interactions in a cationic iron complex. A similar contraction in Fe–C bond distance was observed with dmpe analog between trans-2b and trans-1b (Figure S10, see Supporting Information).

The X-band EPR spectrum of 2a was collected in 2-MeTHF glass at 10 K and exhibited two rhombic signals, consistent with a metal-centered radical and two low-spin S = ½ iron(III) complexes (Figure 1B). The rhombic signal with g-values of 2.54, 2.06 and 1.90 was assigned to the trans isomer of 2a due to the greater axial symmetry in the idealized D2h-symmetric cation. The other rhombic signal with g-values of 2.24, 2.13 and 2.01 was assigned to the cis isomer of 2a, by comparison with the iron(III) cycloneophyl metallacycle 14a with an enforced cis-geometry (vida infra, Figure 4A). These data are consistent with overall cis/trans ratio of 28:72. Likewise, the X-band EPR spectrum for 2b collected under the same conditions also indicated a mixture of cis (g = 2.22, 2.12, 2.02) and trans (g = 2.50, 2.07, 1.92) isomers in a 19:81 ratio (Figure S11, see Supporting Information).

The solid-state, zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectrum collected at 80 K for 2a (Figure 1C) exhibits a major quadrupole doublet (95%) with an isomer shift (δ) of 0.15 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting (|ΔEQ|) of 2.19 mm/s, assigned as the cis isomer of 2a based on comparison with the Mössbauer spectrum of 14a (Figure 4B, vide infra). A minor quadrupole doublet (5%) with a much smaller quadrupole splitting (δ = 0.15 mm/s, |ΔEQ| = 0.33 mm/s) was assigned to trans-2a, where positioning two strong σ-donor ligands in a trans configuration contributes to greater symmetry in electron density. The isomer shifts of both isomers of 2a are consistent with typical values (−0.18 to 0.38 mm/s) for low-spin (S = ½) iron(III) compounds,29 and are similar to those of their iron(II) counterparts (δ = 0.19–0.21 mm/s for 1a).15 Similar Mössbauer parameters were observed for the dmpe-ligated complex 2b, with 95% cis (δ = 0.13 mm/s, |ΔEQ| = 2.15 mm/s) and 5% trans (δ = 0.15 mm/s, |ΔEQ| = 0.17 mm/s) isomers (Figure S12, see Supporting Information). In comparison to 2a and 2b, known [(η5-C5Me5)Fe(P)2(R)]PF6 complexes have higher isomer shifts between 0.25 and 0.55 mm/s (R = CH3, CH2OMe; (P)2 = dppe, (P(OMe)3)2),30 consistent with a reduced s electron density arising from a strongly π-donating η5-C5Me5 ligand.

Overall, the combined spectroscopic evidence suggests that the iron dimethyl complexes 2a and 2b are best described as low-spin S = ½ iron(III) complexes. Moreover, the difference in the cis/trans ratios as detected by EPR and Mössbauer spectroscopies suggests an equilibrium between the cis and trans isomers of the iron(III) dimethyl complexes (eq 1), due to a more labile phosphine arm dissociation from the iron(III) center. This is further corroborated by the difference in the cis/trans isomer ratio between the precursor complex 1a (75:25) and the resultant complex 2a. (1)

### Reactivity of Bis(phosphine) Iron(III) Dimethyl Complexes.

Considering the known reactivity of the ferrous complex, 1a in the C(sp2)–H methylation of arenes with ketone directing groups,15 the analogous reactivity of bis(phosphine) iron(III) dimethyl complexes was investigated. When a THF-d8 solution containing one equivalent of 2a was treated with an excess (10 equiv) of pivalophenone (3a) under a N2 atmosphere, the ortho-methylated arene 4 was not observed after 48 hours at either room temperature or heating to 80 °C (Scheme 3). Instead, a mixture of cationic iron(II) methyl (5) and hydride (6) complexes were detected by 1H and 31P NMR spectroscopies with the concomitant formation of ethylene and methane as organic byproducts. Notably, addition of (Me3P)4Fe(CH3)2 or (depe)2Fe(CH3)(p-tolyl) to a mixture containing 10 equivalents of 3a and one equivalent of [(η5-C5H5)2Fe]BArF4 also produced no observable product 4 after standing at room temperature for 24 hours, despite facile C(sp2)–H methylation mediated by the corresponding iron(II) complexes.10,15

To probe the origin of the lack of arene C–H functionalization by 2a, a series of control experiments was performed (Scheme 4). At 80 °C, heating the neutral iron(II) dimethyl complex 1a with 10 equivalents of arene 3a produced the methylated arene 4 in 90% NMR yield for 24 hours (Scheme 4A). To control for differences in the overall charge, one equivalent of independently synthesized cationic iron(II) methyl complex, 5, was heated with excess 3a at 80 °C for 24 hours. The cyclometallated iron(II) cation 7, resulting from C(sp2)–H activation, was observed by 1H and 31P NMR spectroscopies and isolated in 53% yield along with methane as the byproduct (Scheme 4B). The contrast in reactivity of 2a versus 1a or 5 suggests the oxidation state of the iron center as the dominant factor behind the observed lack of C–H functionalization for 2a, rather than the difference in charge at the iron center (Figure S35, see Supporting Information).

To probe for a potential radical mechanism as the origin of the observed reactivity in Scheme 3, a crossover experiment was conducted (Scheme 5A). A THF-d8 solution containing an equimolar mixture of iron(III) dimethyl complex 2a and iron(III) di(trideuteromethyl) complex 2a-d6 was allowed to stand at room temperature for 120 hours. In addition to natural-abundance methane (CH4) and ethylene (C2H4), mono- and tri-deuteromethane (CH3D and CD3H) were also detected by 1H NMR spectroscopy (Figure S36, see Supporting Information), consistent with the generation of methyl radical arising from Fe(III)–C bond homolysis. This pathway competes against C–H activation reactivity. No evidence for the isotopologs of ethylene, C2HxD4-x (x = 1, 2, 3), was obtained from analysis by 1H NMR spectroscopy, supporting the lack of crossover.

Additional support for the generation of methyl radical derives from mixing one equivalent of a THF-d8 solution of 2a with excess β-pinene (8) as a radical trap. The known ring-opened product 9 was detected in 84% yield by 1H NMR spectroscopy, signaling methyl radical formation (Scheme 5B). A related trapping experiment was conducted with 1,1-diphenylethylene and resulted in detection of the hydromethylation product in 36% yield resulting from methyl radical addition, while treatment with excess TEMPO radical led to the formation of TEMPO–CH3 (Figures S38–40, see Supporting Information). Taken together, the experiments convincingly demonstrate the generation of free methyl radical from 2a.

The experimental observation of methyl radical formation inspired DFT calculations on 2a to determine the strength of the Fe–C bond (Figure 2). On the doublet, quartet and sextet potential energy surfaces (PES), geometries of all ground and transition states were optimized using the TPSS functional and the Karlsruhe def2-TZVP basis set.31,32 With a def2-TZVPP basis set and the SMD (Solvation Model based on Density) implicit solvation model for THF,33 single-point calculations were performed using the TPSSh functional due to its reported accuracy in the prediction of spin-state energies of first-row transition metal complexes.34

For the cis-isomer of 2a (Figure 2), the S = 1/2 doublet, 2[cis-2a] was computed as the ground state, consistent with the experimental data (Figure 1). The quartet and sextet excited states are 21.5 (4[cis-2a]) and 38.5 kcal/mol (6[cis-2a]) higher in energy, respectively. After ligand substitution of one equivalent depe with phenone 3a to form the C(sp2)–H agostic complex, the lowest-energy transition state for C–H activation was located on the doublet surface, 2[cis-TS1], with a barrier of 40.3 kcal/mol. The quartet and sextet transition states are substantially higher in energy at 61.6 and 71.9 kcal/mol, respectively, rendering two-state reactivity unlikely.

In contrast, Fe–C bond homolysis from 2[cis-2a] was found to generate a free methyl radical and a five-coordinate cationic iron(II) methyl complex in the triplet (3[cis-Int1]) or singlet state (1[cis-Int1]) with a calculated bond dissociation free energy (BDFE) of 20.6 or 21.3 kcal/mol, respectively. While attempts to locate transition states for this step were unsuccessful, the barriers for bond homolysis reactions are close to the BDFE without complications from steric constraints or spin state changes.35 Therefore, with an approximate ΔΔG‡ of 19.7 kcal/mol, Fe–C bond homolysis from cis-2a is predicted to be significantly more facile than C–H activation. Similarly, an approximate ΔΔG‡ of 20.8 kcal/mol favoring Fe–C bond homolysis (calculated BDFE = 26.8 kcal/mol) over C–H activation (ΔG‡ = 47.6 kcal/mol) was computed for trans-2a (Figure S93, see Supporting Information).

Taken together, the experimental and computational results support a facile Fe–C bond homolysis pathway as the rationale for the observed lack of arene C–H methylation mediated by iron(III) dimethyl complex 2a and a plausible mechanism for the observed reaction outcomes is proposed in Scheme 6. Starting from the cis-isomer of 2a, Fe–C bond homolysis outcompetes the slower C–H activation, affording a coordinatively unsaturated iron(II) methyl cation, cis-Int1, and a methyl radical. Dinitrogen coordination to the fluxional five-coordinate cis-Int1 affords the observed complex 5, whereas reaction of the cage-escaped methyl radical with another equivalent of cis-2a generates methane and a putative six-coordinate cationic iron methyl methylene complex, cis-Int2. The fleeting cis-Int2 intermediate is proposed to undergo facile ⍺-migratory insertion and the resulting iron ethyl cation, cis-Int3, is converted to the cationic iron(II) hydride (6) following β-hydride elimination and ligand substitution of the ethylene byproduct by dinitrogen. Because the BDFE of Fe–C bond in trans-2a is calculated to be 6.2 kcal/mol higher than that in cis-2a and since cis and trans isomers of 2a are in equilibrium (eq 1), it is proposed that trans-2a is first isomerized to cis-2a and then deactivated by Fe–C bond homolysis.

### Mechanism-Inspired Development of C–H Activating Iron(III) Complex.

To circumvent the competing Fe–C homolysis pathway for iron(III) dialkyl complexes and favor C–H functionalization, cationic iron(III) diaryl complexes, [P4FeAr2]+ were targeted as Fe–C(sp2) bonds are typically less prone to homolysis (Scheme 7A).15,35,36 However, treatment of a diethyl ether solution of (depe)2Fe(4-tolyl)2 (10) with one equivalent of [(η5-C5H5)2Fe][BArF4] oxidant in diethyl ether at room temperature did not lead to the isolation of the desired cationic iron(III) diaryl cation complex. Instead, [(depe)3Fe][BArF4] (11) and 4,4’-dimethylbiphenyl were observed by a combination 1H NMR and EPR spectroscopies along with other unidentified iron complexes (Figures S41–S43, see Supporting Information). The connectivity of 11 established by X-ray diffraction supports an idealized octahedral geometry.

In-situ generation of iron(III) diaryl cation was also attempted by addition of 1 equivalent of 10 to a THF-d8 solution containing 1 equivalent of [(η5-C5H5)2Fe][BArF4] and 10 equivalents of 3a. Again, formation of 11 and 4,4’-dimethylbiphenyl was observed without detectable evidence for C(sp2)–H arylation of 3a. Overall, these results demonstrate that C(sp2)–C(sp2) reductive elimination is preferred for iron(III) diaryl complexes, outcompeting the desired, bimolecular C–H functionalization process. Rapid C–C reductive elimination from iron(III) complexes has been previously experimentally demonstrated and supported by computational studies.13,15,23,26

To slow C–C reductive elimination and suppress alkyl radical formation through chelation, tethering the two organometallic ligands was proposed as a strategy. Consequently, the reactivity in C–H activation of iron(III) metallacyclopentane was investigated (Scheme 7B). Addition of one equivalent of [(η5-C5H5)2Fe][BArF4] to a THF-d8 solution of (depe)2Fe(CH2)4 (12) (Figure S45, see Supporting Information) in the presence of 10 equivalents of pivalophenone 3a resulted in the complete conversion of the iron(II) metallacycle after 15 minutes at ambient temperature, as judged by 1H and 31P NMR spectroscopies. The iron(III) metallacyclopentane cation with paramagnetically broadened and shifted 1H NMR resonances resembling those of the iron(III) dimethyl complex 2a was observed and converted over the course of 24 hours to ethylene and unidentified iron byproducts, without detectable evidence for the C–H alkylation of arene 3a (Figures S46–48, see Supporting Information). This in turn suggests a retro cycloaddition pathway being favored over arene C–H activation. Reductive ring opening from an iron(III) center (and its reverse reaction, oxidative cyclization) has been extensively studied by our laboratory for the iron(III) alkyl-allyl metallacycle supported by a monoreduced radical anionic pincer.37

To increase the lifetime of the iron(III) intermediate and to promote C(sp2)–H activation, an iron(III) alkyl-aryl metallacycle was targeted (Figure 3). Inspirations were drawn from our recent reports on facile and chemoselective arene C(sp2)–H functionalization mediated by the non-metallacyclic iron(II) methyl aryl complex, trans-(depe)2Fe(CH3)(4-R-C6H4) (R = H, Me, OMe, NMe2),15 as well as by the bis(phosphine)-ligated cobalt(III) alkyl-aryl metallacycles.38 Given its known ability to stabilize Group 9–10 metals of moderate to high oxidation states,39 the cycloneophyl complex was pursued. Design principles were incorporated to suppress competing pathways. These include: (i) tethering the alkyl and the aryl groups to disfavor homolysis of the Fe–C(sp3) bond; (ii) gem-dimethyl substitution in the β-position to prevent elimination; (iii) reductive ring opening from the alkyl-aryl metallacycle due to the instability of the free aryne; and (iv) the five-membered chelate to raise the barrier to C(sp2)–C(sp3) reductive elimination.

### Synthesis of Iron(III) Cycloneophyl Metallacycle Complexes.

Synthesis of the depe-ligated metallacycle commenced by addition of Mg(CH2CMe2Ph)40 to a diethyl ether solution of (depe)2FeCl2 for one hour at ambient temperature followed by heating to 50 °C for 16 hours in a closed vessel (Scheme 8A). This procedure furnished neutral iron(II) cycloneophyl complex, 13a, in 33% yield. The 31P{1H} NMR spectrum of the diamagnetic iron compound in benzene-d6 exhibited a set of four equal-area multiplets between 76.0 and 59.0 ppm, consistent with an octahedral iron(II) metallacycle.

Addition of one equivalent of [(η5-C5H5)2Fe][BArF4] to a diethyl ether solution of 13a furnished 14a as a greyish-green crystalline solid in 69% isolated yield. The 1H NMR spectrum of 14a in THF-d8 exhibited paramagnetically broadened resonances between 15.0 and −15.0 ppm. The solid-state structure was determined by X-ray diffraction and contained significant disorder in the depe ligand and the BArF4 anion but the connectivity supported the assignment of 14a with an idealized octahedral geometry and cis bidentate phosphines.

The X-band EPR spectrum of 14a was recorded in 2-MeTHF glass at 10 K and exhibited a rhombic signal with g-values of 2.36, 2.29 and 1.95 (Figure 4A), consistent with an overall S = ½ iron(III) complex. The zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectrum recorded at 80 K featured an asymmetric quadrupole doublet with δ = 0.24 mm/s and |ΔEQ| = 2.23 mm/s (Figure 4B). The isomer shift of 14a is close to those of 2a and 2b (vide supra) and within the range of values for known S = ½ iron(III) compounds.29 The band asymmetry in the quadrupole doublet observed for 2a, 2b, and 14a has been observed in other known iron(III) complexes due to paramagnetic relaxation.29,30 The combined spectroscopic data supports the assignment of 14a as a low-spin S = ½ iron(III) complex.

To gain additional structural insights on the iron(III) cycloneophyl metallacycle, synthesis of the more crystalline, dmpe-coordinated variant, 14b, was also targeted (Scheme 8B). Dialkylation of (dcype)FeCl2 with one equivalent of Mg(CH2CMe2Ph)2 in diethyl ether afforded the paramagnetic iron(II) dialkyl complex 15 in quantitative yield after 1 hour at room temperature.41 Subsequent stirring with three equivalents of dmpe ligand at room temperature for 24 hours resulted in the formation of the dmpe-coordinated iron(II) cycloneophyl complex (13b), as judged by 1H and 31P NMR spectroscopies. Direct oxidation of crude 13b with [(η5-C5H5)2Fe][BArF4] followed by trituration with pentane afforded the iron(III) cycloneophyl complex 14b in 89% yield over 2 steps. Notably, attempts at direct alkylation-cyclometallation starting from (dmpe)2FeCl2 – analogous to the synthesis of 13a – yielded only trace amounts of 13b, likely a consequence of the low lability of the smaller dmpe chelate.42 Separately, recrystallization of 13b from pentane at −35 °C afforded yellow-orange crystals and X-ray diffraction confirmed the identity of 13b as a neutral iron(II) cycloneophyl with an idealized octahedral geometry (Figure 4C).

Like 14a, 14b exhibits paramagnetically broadened 1H NMR resonances and a rhombic X-band EPR spectrum with g-values of 2.32, 2.18 and 1.98 (Figure S29, see Supporting Information). Dark grey crystals of 14b suitable for X-ray diffraction were obtained from a saturated diethyl ether solution at −35 °C. The solid-state structure confirmed its assignment as a low-spin S = ½ iron(III) compound with an idealized octahedral geometry (Figure 4C). Analogous to the iron(III) dimethyl cations 2a and 2b, both Fe–Calkyl (2.097(4) Å) and Fe–Caryl (2.009(4) Å) bonds was contracted in 14b relative to those in the corresponding iron(II) complex 13b – 2.1154(13) Å and 2.0282(13) Å, respectively.

### Reactivity of Iron(III) Cycloneophyl Complexes towards C–H Functionalization.

With isolable iron(III) metallacycles in hand, the hypotheses illustrated in Figure 3 were evaluated. Addition of 10 equivalents of pivalophenone (3a) to a THF-d8 solution of 14a resulted in 97% yield of the desired alkylated product after 16 hours at ambient temperature (Scheme 9A). The product of C–H alkylation (16a) was preferred over C–H arylation (17a) with near exclusive selectivity, with the iron(I) dinitrogen complex, [(depe)2Fe(N2)]BArF4 (18), identified as the iron product. When 14a was generated in situ from stoichiometric amounts of 13a and [(η5-C5H5)2Fe][BArF4] in the presence of 10 equivalents of 3a at room temperature, a near quantitative yield of C–H functionalized arenes was also observed after the same duration with similar chemoselectivity (16a:17a = 94:6).

By comparison, the iron(II) metallacycle 13a produced no detectable reaction in the presence of excess 3a at room temperature after 16 hours. Heating to 80 °C afforded the ortho-C(sp2)–H functionalized products in a combined 99% yield after 16 hours (Scheme 9B), suggesting a substantially lower barrier for the iron(III)-mediated transformation than the iron(II) equivalent. An erosion in chemoselectivity was observed as a 57:43 mixture of 16a:17a was obtained.

The effect of ligand sterics on iron(III)-mediated C(sp2)–H functionalization was also examined. The iron(III) metallacycle 14b supported by the smaller and less labile dmpe ligand was unreactive with 3a at room temperature, while heating to 80 °C enabled C–H functionalization to exclusively afford the ortho-alkylation product 16a in 59% yield (Scheme 9C). Comparison of the reactivity between 14a and 14b establishes the effect of ligand lability on iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization and supports phosphine dissociation prior to the rate-determining step. Likewise, the dmpe-supported iron(II) cycloneophyl complex (13b) was unreactive in C–H functionalization of 3a at both ambient and elevated temperatures without observable consumption of 13b, consistent with the rate acceleration in C–H functionalization from iron(II) to iron(III) observed for the depe-ligated metallacycles 13a and 14a.

The improved activity and selectivity observed with iron(III)-mediated C(sp2)–H functionalization motivated exploration of the scope of the transformation (Scheme 10). In comparison to ketone 3a, an amide directing group (benzamide 3b) produced facile C–H functionalization, affording exclusively the ortho-alkylation product 16b in 96% yield after 30 minutes at room temperature and without any detectable amount of the C–H arylated arene 17b. The transformation also tolerated a secondary amide (3c) containing an acidic N–H bond, affording exclusively the ortho-alkylation product 16c in 80% yield.

Reaction with more strongly coordinating, N(sp2)-containing directing groups (3d-h) also proceeded at room temperature, affording C–H functionalization products in good to excellent yields (64–95%). Notably, while pyrazole (3d) and benzo[h]quinoline (3e) directing groups enabled exclusive formation of the ortho-alkylation products 16d (95% yield) and 16e (98% yield), the chemoselectivity eroded for oxazoline (3f), pyridine (3g) and imine (3h) directing groups, furnishing a mixture of alkylation and arylation products (16f:17f = 74:26, 16g:17g = 51:49 and 16h:17h = 90:10), with ortho-alkylation being the major product. With the previously reported (depe)2Fe(CH3)(Ar) complexes, N(sp2)-directed C–H activation afforded the cyclometallated complex after facile C–H activation at room temperature, but oxidation to iron(III) (or heating to 80 °C) was required to accelerate C–C coupling.15 This consequently suggests the ability to mediate more rapid C–C reductive elimination as a key factor behind the observed one-electron differentiation in C–H functionalization reactivity between iron(II) and iron(III).

With an aldehyde (3i), ester (3j) or sulfoxide (3k) directing group, no reaction was observed at room temperature for 12 hours, while heating at 80 °C for 12 hours afforded the respective C–H alkylation products 16i, 16j and 16k in 20%, 42% and 40% yields. In contrast, C–H functionalization of aryl amides and esters was not observed for iron(II) methyl aryl complexes (depe)2Fe(CH3)(Ar) even after extended heating at 80–110 °C.15 Combined with the observed sluggish reactivity of the analogous iron(II) metallacycle (Scheme 9B), the more facile iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization is also compatible with a wider scope of directing groups than the corresponding iron(II) variant.

The ability of iron(III) to functionalize substrates containing directing groups located at varied distances from the C–H bond of interest was also demonstrated. In the presence of two accessible C–H bonds at C2 and C8 in quinoline (3l), exclusive alkylation at C8 was observed after incubation at 80 °C for 12 hours, furnishing the 8-neophylated product (16l) in 95% yield. Meanwhile, the acetanilide 3m, which is highly reactive in palladium-mediated C–H activation, showed sluggish reactivity even at 80 °C, affording 28% of the ortho-alkylation product 16m after 12 hours.

The one-electron differentiation in reactivity and selectivity between iron(II) and iron(III) was also demonstrated across several directing groups. With the pyridine-like N-directing group in benzo[h]quinoline (3e), C–H functionalization mediated by the iron(II) cycloneophyl complex, 13a, required harsher conditions (80 °C, 12 h) and was less selective, yielding alkylation (16e) and arylation (17e) products in a 62:38 ratio (Figure S55, see Supporting Information). In comparison, 16e was obtained exclusively in 98% yield after 1 hour at 23 °C with the iron(III) cycloneophyl 14a. Meanwhile, iron(II) cycloneophyl showed no reactivity with amide (3b), oxazoline (3f), ester (3j), or sulfoxide (3k) groups, both at 23 °C and 80 °C.

Attempted C–H functionalization with typical weakly coordinating directing groups,43 including furan, thiophene, nitro, sulfonamide, amine, and ether, proved unsuccessful at both room and elevated temperatures (Chart S1, see Supporting Information). In these cases, competing deactivation of 14a by C(sp2)–C(sp3) reductive elimination to form iron(I) complex 18 and 7,7-dimethylbicyclo[4.2.0]octa-1,3,5-triene was observed instead (after 72 hours at 80 °C).

### Mechanistic Investigations.

As the observed one-electron differentiation in both reactivity and chemoselectivity of arene C–H functionalization mediated by iron(III) and iron(II) metallacycles has rarely been reported in the literature, mechanistic investigations were conducted to uncover its origin. Using the variable time normalization analysis (VTNA) technique developed by Burés and coworkers,44 the experimental rate law was derived for the reaction between iron(III) metallacycle 14a and pivalophenone 3a at 23 °C in THF-d8. By separately varying the concentrations of 3a and 14a, a first-order rate dependence on both the arene and the iron(III) complex was established (Figures S65 and S67, see Supporting Information). Reaction inhibition by free depe ligand was observed and an inverse first-order rate dependence on depe concentration was determined (Figure S69, see Supporting Information). The experimental rate law derived (eq 2) is consistent with the involvement of reversible phosphine dissociation prior to the rate-determining step. Additional mechanistic insights were gleaned from deuterium kinetic isotope effect (KIE) experiments. In two separate J. Young NMR tubes, one equivalent of 14a was added to a THF-d8 solution containing 10 equivalents of pivalophenone 3a with one equivalent of 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene as an internal standard (Scheme 11A). Monitoring the initial rates of the reaction by the formation of the respective C–H alkylation products (16a or 16a-d5 and isotopologs) by 1H NMR spectroscopy provided a kH/kD ratio of 1.0(1), suggesting minimal involvement of C–H bond cleavage in the rate-determining step. An intermolecular competition experiment was performed with one equivalent of 14a and 10 equivalents of 3a and 3a-d5 each in the same J. Young NMR tube (Scheme 11B). Analysis of the ratio of products 16a and 16a-d5 (and its isotopologs) by 1H NMR spectroscopy at 10–20% conversion provided a kH/kD value of 2.0(1) at 23 °C.

Preparative deuterium labeling experiments provided additional insights on the nature of the iron(III)-mediated C–H activation step (Scheme 11C). A THF-d8 mixture of one equivalent of 14a and 10 equivalents of 3a-d5 reached completion after 16 hours at 23 °C. Analysis by 1H NMR spectroscopy established the formation of the C(sp2)–H alkylation product (16a-dn) in 97% yield, with no detectable deuterium incorporation in the benzylic position. The C–H/D bonds ortho- to the pivaloyl group in both the remaining pivalophenone 3a-dn and product 16a-dn retained 88% and 92% deuterium abundance, respectively. Considering the 1:10 stoichiometric ratio of 14a and 3a, this is consistent with the 95% deuterium incorporation observed at both ortho-carbon atoms of the neophyl phenyl group in the product (16a-dn). Taken together, the results of the KIE and deuterium labeling experiments support reversible C(sp2)–H activation by the Fe(III)–Caryl bond in 14a prior to the rate-determining step.45 The lack of benzylic deuteration in the alkylated arene implies that C(sp2)–H activation by the Fe(III)–Calkyl bond is significantly slower than that by the Fe(III)–Caryl bond, which is analogous to the orbital hybridization effect observed for C(sp2)–H methylation mediated by related iron(II) complexes.15

Possible pathways for iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization were also studied by full molecule DFT calculations. For the iron(III) cycloneophyl cation 14a, a doublet ground state was located with the quartet (+16.1 kcal/mol) and sextet (+40.2 kcal/mol) excited states significantly higher in energy (Figure 5A). The optimized geometry of the dmpe-supported iron(III) metallacycle 14b was consistent with the solid-state structure determined experimentally (Table S2, see Supporting Information). All isomers of the iron(III) complexes during the C–H functionalization pathway were considered and computed with only the lowest-energy isomer for each spin state presented.

Beginning with 14a, dissociation of one phosphine arm to form [(κ1-depe)(κ2-depe)Fe(cycloneophyl)]+ (Int3) is endergonic by +13.1 kcal/mol on the doublet surface (i.e., 2[Int3]). Int3 also has a lower-lying quartet ground state (4[Int3], +11.7 kcal/mol), and a substantially higher lying sextet excited state, 6[Int3] (+40.1 kcal/mol). By comparison, homolysis of Fe–Calkyl or Fe–Caryl bond from 2[14a] is less thermodynamically favorable, due to the more positive ΔG° incurred (28.6 and 45.2 kcal/mol, respectively). Subsequent dissociation of the κ1-depe ligand and coordination of the arene substrate 3a leads to the formation of the iron(III) C–H agostic complex, Int4, with a doublet ground state 2[Int4] (+18.8 kcal/mol) and an energetically similar quartet excited state 4[Int4] (+19.8 kcal/mol). It should be noted that the ΔG° for the formation of Int4 (+18.8 kcal/mol) is much less endergonic than those calculated (~ +30 kcal/mol) for the iron(II) C–H agostic complex in our previous study.15 The lack of observation of an iron(III) C–H agostic complex by 1H NMR spectroscopy during the reaction is consistent with the DFT prediction that Int4 is energetically uphill and not formed in appreciable quantities relative to 14a.

Proceeding from Int4 towards C–H activation and C–C coupling, a bifurcation in the reaction pathway was considered to account for the observed chemoselectivity. Formation of the C(sp2)–H arylation product (17a) commences with C(sp2)–H cleavage by the Fe(III)–Caryl bond (Figure 5B, towards right). On the doublet PES, a four-centered σ-CAM transition state 2[TS2] was located, which lies 9.8 kcal/mol above 2[Int4] and +28.6 kcal/mol from the starting substrates. In comparison, transition state structures of TS2 located on the quartet and sextet surfaces are sufficiently higher in energy (+55.7 and +70.0 kcal/mol, respectively). Attempt to locate transition states for an alternative oxidative addition pathway involving the iron(III/V) redox couple was unsuccessful and converged to the redox-neutral σ-CAM transition states.

The C–H activation step was computed to be moderately exergonic with a ΔG° of −2.6 kcal/mol. The immediate product is computed to be an iron(III) η2-C(sp2)–H σ-agostic complex on the quartet PES (4[Int5], +16.2 kcal/mol) with a nearly degenerate doublet excited state, 2[Int5] (+16.4 kcal/mol). Distinct from the C–H cleavage step, C(sp2)–C(sp3) reductive elimination to form the C(sp2)–H alkylation product 16a was calculated to proceed preferentially through an intermediate quartet spin transition state 4[TS3] with a barrier of 14.3 kcal/mol relative to 4[Int5] and an overall ΔG‡ of +30.5 kcal/mol. C(sp2)–C(sp3) formation through either the doublet or sextet transition state is less plausible due to greater computed ΔG‡ of +37.5 (2[Int5]) and +56.2 kcal/mol (6[Int5]).

For C(sp2)–H cleavage mediated by the Fe(III)–Calkyl bond (Figure 5B, towards left), an analogous σ-CAM transition state, 2[TS4] (+34.5 kcal/mol), was located on the doublet PES, 15.7 kcal/mol uphill from 2[Int4], with negligible involvement of the higher-lying quartet and sextet transition states, 4[TS4] (+55.1 kcal/mol) and 6[TS4] (+66.9 kcal/mol). The resultant iron(III) η2-C(sp3)–H σ-agostic complex was also predicted to possess a quartet ground state, 4[Int6] (+14.5 kcal/mol), with a thermally accessible doublet excited state, 4[Int6] (+19.2 kcal/mol). Subsequent C(sp2)–C(sp2) reductive elimination was computed to go through a quartet transition state, 4[TS3] (+27.7 kcal/mol).

Overall, the C(sp2)–H alkylation pathway has a barrier of 30.5 kcal/mol with C(sp2)–C(sp3) reductive elimination as the rate-determining step after reversible phosphine dissociation and C(sp2)–H activation steps. The computed pathway corroborates the empirically derived rate law (eq 2), the deuterium KIE and labeling experiments (Scheme 11). In comparison, the minor C(sp2)–H arylation pathway incurs a barrier of 34.5 kcal/mol with a rate-determining C(sp2)–H activation step. The overall ΔΔG‡ of 4.0 kcal/mol in favor of the formation of the C(sp2)–C(sp3) coupling product 16a is largely consistent with the empirically observed 16a:17a ratio of >99:1 In terms of the C–H cleavage alone, the ΔΔG‡ between 2[TS2] and 2[TS4] amounts to 5.9 kcal/mol, which is consistent with the observed lack of deuterium incorporation at the benzylic methylene position of 16a-dn in the isotopic labeling experiment (Scheme 11C).

### Proposed Mechanism.

Based on both the experimental and computational results, a mechanism for the iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization of arene 3a is proposed (Scheme 12). Reversible and facile bis(phosphine) arm dissociation from the octahedral S = ½ complex 14a opens a vacant site in the five-coordinate intermediate Int3 for the coordination of the substrate 3a. Full dissociation of a depe ligand then leads to the reversible formation of the putative C–H agostic complex Int4. From Int4, reversible C–H cleavage mediated by the Fe(III)–Caryl bond in TS2 is significantly more facile than that by the Fe(III)–Calkyl bond in TS4. This reactivity pattern is consistent with the hybridization effect recently established for a redox-neutral σ-CAM transition state involving dn>0 transition metal centers.15 From the resultant η2-(C–H) σ-agostic complex (Int5), rate-determining C(sp2)–C(sp3) reductive elimination affords the ortho-C–H alkylation product 16a as the major organic product, while dinitrogen coordination to the unsaturated post-reductive-elimination iron(I) intermediate generates 18 as the inorganic byproduct. Distinct from the reported iron(II) methyl aryl system with C–H activation as the rate- and selectivity-determining step15, the iron(III) cycloneophyl features reversible C–H cleavage and rate-determining C–C reductive elimination steps.

## DISCUSSION

### Well-Defined Organometallic Iron(III) Complexes.

Well-defined organometallic ferric complexes are rare in the literature and most examples are supported by porphyrin or cyclopentadienyl ligands with early examples being characterized by Balch and Astruc, respectively (Chart 2).46,47 Homoleptic iron(III) polyhydrocarbyl-ate complexes,27c,27d,27e and cyclometallated iron(III) complexes are also known.48 By comparison, the synthesis of phosphine-ligated iron(III) hydrocarbyl complexes remain scarce, despite a number of examples of iron(III) halides and thiolates.49 Accordingly, the reactivity of well-defined organometallic iron(III) complexes especially in mediating C–H functionalization reactions has not been studied.

In this study, a host of six-coordinate bis(phosphine) iron(III) organometallic complexes were reported and organometallic iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization was demonstrated with iron(III) cycloneophyl 14a. Mechanistic studies have established a redox-neutral σ-CAM pathway for C–H activation on the low-spin (doublet) PES, as well as a spin crossover onto the intermediate-spin (quartet) PES for more favorable C–C reductive elimination.

### Directing Group Effects in Iron(III)-Mediated C–H Functionalization.

Closer inspection of the results of iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization with different directing groups (Scheme 10) established a positive correlation between the basicity of the directing group (using reported pKaH values for first-order approximation)50 and the rate of arene C–H functionalization mediated by iron(III) cycloneophyl complex 14a (Figure 6A). A non-basic nitro directing group (pKaH = −12.4) failed to enable C–H functionalization despite prolonged reflux in THF-d8. By comparison, ester (3j) and aldehyde (3i) groups with less negative pKaH values between −6 and −7 were more reactive but prolonged heating was required to obtain moderate yields. Ketones (3a) underwent reaction at room temperature, consistent with a more Lewis basic carbonyl oxygen owing to a more electron-donating alkyl substituent (compared to aldehyde). In contrast, when the pKaH value of a directing group exceeds 0, the C–H functionalization reaction was rapid and reached completion within 1 hour at room temperature as observed with amide (3b) and imine/pyridine-like N(sp2) directing groups (3d-3h) with pKaH between 0 and 6. These observations corroborate reports by Nakamura, Ilies, and coworkers, where iron-catalyzed C(sp2)–H arylation with pyridines, pyrazoles, and imines proceeded between 0 and 30 °C,23a,51 supports the potential involvement of redox-neutral C–H activation by an organometallic iron(III) intermediate.

The selectivity for ortho C(sp2)–H alkylation versus arylation decreased as the basicity of directing groups increased. Exclusive or high selectivity for C(sp2)–C(sp2) coupling products 16 was observed for ester (3j), aldehyde (3i), ketone (3a), amide (3b) and pyrazole (3d) directing groups, whereas a mixture of 16 and 17 were obtained in the presence of more strongly coordinating oxazoline, pyridine and imine groups (3f-3h).

These empirical trends on rate and chemoselectivity are consistent with the proposed mechanism (Scheme 12). More Lewis basic directing groups coordinate more readily to iron(III) center in Int3, thus increasing the concentration of the C–H agostic complex Int4, accelerating the overall reaction. In the transition states of the C–H activation step accounting for the observed chemoselectivity (TS2 and TS4), the directing group is preferably positioned trans to the Fe–C bond not responsible for cleaving the C–H bond. A more σ-donating N(sp2) directing group destabilizes both transition states by virtue of a stronger Pauli repulsion between trans ligands.52 Due to the stronger σ-donacity of an alkyl ligand (trans to directing group in TS2) than aryl ligand (trans to directing group in TS4),53 greater destabilization of TS2 (leading to C–H alkylation) is expected than that of TS4 (responsible for C–H arylation). This thus contributes to the observed erosion in the chemoselectivity for C–H alkylation versus arylation for substrates 3f-3h.

While the effect of coordinating ability of directing groups on the rate of C–H functionalization has been studied extensively with precious metal complexes (Pd, Ir, Ru, Rh), fewer investigations have been conducted with first-row transition metals.54 For iron chemistry, catalytic results have suggested that the reactivity towards C–H activation decreases in the order of bidentate monoanionic, monodentate monoanionic, and monodentate neutral directing groups.55 For example, in iron-catalyzed directed C–H arylation reactions developed by Nakamura, Ilies and co-workers, N-quinolinyl amides (bidentate monoanionic) were more reactive than N-aryl secondary amides (monodentate monoanionic),56 followed by tertiary amides (monodentate neutral).57 The observed reactivity trends with directing group variation are consistent with the results of this study, suggesting the potential involvement of an analogous iron(III)-mediated σ-CAM C–H activation in these catalytic reactions. Furthermore, our study serves as a rare systematic demonstration and rationalization of the effect of varying directing groups – especially monodentate neutral ones – on both the rate and chemoselectivity of the iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization.

The preferred site of iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization was highly sensitive to the distance from the directing group (Figure 6B). Compared to room-temperature activation of the C10–H bond in benzo[h]quinoline (3e), functionalization of the C8–H bond in quinoline (3i) required significantly harsher conditions, while the C2 site in 3i remained unreactive. A similar comparison was found between benzamide 3b and acetanilide 3m, where the more facile functionalization of the former than the latter was observed (Scheme 10). Taken together, these results suggest a potentially innate preference for the formation of 5-membered cyclometallated intermediates during iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization processes. Notably, our results complement reports by Nakamura, Ilies and coworkers on the sensitivity of catalytic reactivity to the directing group geometry – specifically, the H3C–C–C(=O) angle – in the iron-catalyzed C(sp3)–H arylation of N-quinolinyl amides,56 further emphasizing geometric selectivity as a distinctive feature of iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization.

In contrast, Pd(II)-mediated C–H functionalization, which proceeds by a distinct concerted metalation-deprotonation mechanism, has been shown to be less sensitive to the distance between the directing group and the site of C–H activation.43 In this regard, our study has demonstrated the complementarity of iron(III)-mediated C–H functionalization with the promise of greater site selectivity.

### Oxidation State-Dependent Reactivity of Transition Metal Complexes.

It was established that metal centers of the same element but different oxidation states are able to mediate reactions of different types.53 With the increasing emphasis and utility of 3d transition metal catalysis, understanding and utilizing their intrinsically higher density of states and greater preference for one-electron reaction pathways will offer invaluable insights for the development of green and sustainable catalysis and methodologies.3a

Examples of rate changes of the same reaction as a function of metal oxidation state have been reported, for instance, in nickel-catalyzed cross coupling58 and cobalt-catalyzed asymmetric hydrogenation.59 For bipyridine-supported iron alkyl complexes, Kochi has demonstrated the contrasting preferences of iron(II), iron(III) and iron(IV) oxidation states for β-hydride elimination, Fe–C bond homolysis, and C–C reductive elimination, respectively.60 Meanwhile, rate acceleration in iron(III)-mediated insertion into CO ligand61 as well as hydrogen atom transfer to olefins62 versus their iron(II) counterparts have been experimentally observed and/or computationally proposed. However, the mechanistic origin of such one-electron differentiated rate acceleration is typically not well understood and the effects on the chemoselectivity rarely investigated.

By comparison, this study demonstrates a rare example where both the rate and chemoselectivity of transition metal-mediated C–H functionalization are altered by one-electron changes in the oxidation state of the metal center (Figure 7). Experimental and computational investigations support a mechanistic rationale for the observed reactivity. As evident from the studies on imine/pyridine-like N(sp2) directing groups, a significantly lowered barrier to C–C reductive elimination from iron(III) over iron(II) counterpart serves an important explanation for the rate acceleration in the iron(III) system. An increased lability of bis(phosphine) ligands and a more cationic and electrophilic iron(III) center in turn facilitate substrate coordination and favor the formation of the η2-C–H agostic complex, which was computationally suggested as >10 kcal/mol less exergonic than the reported iron(II) systems (Figure 5).15

With respect to chemoselectivity, the effect of orbital hybridization initially established for iron(II) systems also proved applicable to iron(III)-mediated C–H activation, as both traverse a redox-neutral σ-CAM-type transition state.15 Specifically, C–H activation by an Fe–C(sp2) bond was favored over that by Fe–C(sp3), as a lower reorganization energy was required to form the σ-CAM transition state, due to the lower directionality and higher partial s character of the Fe–C(sp2) bond. In addition, the iron(III)-mediated transformation was characterized by a distinct regime of reversible C–H activation and rate-determining C(sp2)–C(sp3) activation. Notably, the computational data supports a more pronounced hybridization effect with the iron(III) cycloneophyl system, with a ΔΔG‡ of 5.9 kcal/mol in the C–H cleavage step, as compared to a ΔΔG‡ of 2.1 kcal/mol in the previously reported iron(II) system.15 Overall, these results corroborate the observed changes in chemoselectivity of C–C coupling in the products formed.

## CONCLUSIONS

Examples of organometallic C–H functionalization of arenes mediated by well-defined bis(phosphine)-supported iron(III) hydrocarbyl complexes have been reported in this study. The mechanistically inspired design principles that promote efficient C–H functionalization at iron(III) centers were illustrated by combined experimental and computational investigations. Iron(III) dialkyl and diaryl cations were unreactive in C–H functionalization due to competing Fe–C bond homolysis and C–C reductive elimination, respectively, while iron(III) dialkyl metallacycles were prone to reductive ring opening. Inspired by these observations, cationic iron(III) neophyl metallacycles were synthesized, capable of mediating C(sp2)–H functionalization with substantially faster rate and greater chemoselectivity than the iron(II) counterpart. The ligand effect was examined, where decreasing ligand lability correlates with a higher barrier. Iron(III) metallacycle-mediated C–H functionalization also exhibited a broader functional group compatibility than the iron(II) systems with directing groups, including ketone, amide, pyridine and ester. The rate law, deuterium labeling and kinetic isotope effect experiments and computational modeling support a reversible C–H activation step followed by rate-determining C(sp2)–C(sp3) reductive elimination. The one-electron differentiated reactivity and selectivity is attributed to the synergistic effects of increased ligand lability, less exergonic substrate coordination, enhanced orbital hybridization effect in C–H activation and more facile C–C reductive elimination.
